claims.claim: Spontaneous spike-like events resembled synaptically evoked spikes in shape, including a clear inflection at spike initiation.
claims.source: Occasionally we observed spontaneous spike-like events, which resembled synaptically evoked spikes in shape, including a clear inflection at spike initiation (Figure 2g–h).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The average spontaneous spike amplitude and area were 17.78 ± 2.09 mV and 9941 ± 2640 mV*ms respectively (n = 22 spikes).
claims.source: The average spontaneous spike amplitude and area were 17.78 ± 2.09 mV and 9941 ± 2640 mV*ms respectively (n = 22 spikes).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claims.claim: Addition of MK801 to the patch pipette solution completely blocked dendritic spikes.
claims.source: Addition of MK801 to the patch pipette solution completely blocked dendritic spikes (Figure 2e).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The spike amplitude and area at just-suprathreshold stimulation intensity was reduced to 32.7 ± 5.3% and 17.2 ± 2.2% respectively with intracellular MK801 (n = 6 cells; 40 min after patch breakthrough).
claims.source: The spike amplitude and area at just-suprathreshold stimulation intensity was reduced to 32.7 ± 5.3% and 17.2 ± 2.2% respectively (n = 6 cells; 40 min after patch breakthrough).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claims.claim: NMDA spikes were accompanied by large calcium transients around the activated dendritic site.
claims.source: Dendritic calcium imaging revealed that NMDA spikes were accompanied by large calcium transients around the activated dendritic site (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Large calcium transients were seen only in the stimulated branches; calcium transients in unstimulated branches remained low.
claims.source: Large calcium transients were seen only in the stimulated branches; calcium transients in unstimulated branches remained low (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: A maximal calcium transient at the activated dendritic location fell off steeply in both proximal and distal directions relative to the activated sites.
claims.source: Using OGB-6F we observed a maximal calcium transient at the activated dendritic location which fell off steeply in both proximal and distal directions relative to the activated sites (Figure 3b–e).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The calcium profile data are consistent with NMDA spike-evoked calcium profiles seen in basal dendrites of layer five pyramidal neurons, and indicate the initiation of a local, non-actively propagated spike.
claims.source: These data are consistent with NMDA spike-evoked calcium profiles seen in basal dendrites of layer five pyramidal neurons, and indicate the initiation of a local, non-actively propagated spike (Major et al., 2008; Schiller et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Pyramidal neurons in PCx receive a much larger number of inputs from IC axons in the deeper layers than from bulb inputs conveyed by the LOT in layer 1a.
claims.source: In addition to bulb inputs conveyed by the LOT in layer 1a, pyramidal neurons in PCx receive a much larger number of inputs from IC axons in the deeper layers (Haberly, 2001; Haberly and Price, 1978; Johnson et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Spikes could be generated throughout the LOT-recipient zone in layer 1a, but also in layers 1b and two where pyramidal neurons primarily receive intracortical inputs.
claims.source: We found that spikes could not only be generated throughout the LOT-recipient zone in layer 1a, but also in layers 1b and two where pyramidal neurons primarily receive intracortical inputs (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The amplitude of NMDA spikes recorded at the soma increased significantly (from 6.4 ± 0.7 mV to 25.9 ± 3.1 mV) as the uncaging site moved from distal (318.6 ± 7.9 µm) to proximal (99 ± 14.6 µm) dendritic locations (p = 0.00014).
claims.source: In keeping with previous reports (Major et al., 2008), the amplitude of NMDA spikes recorded at the soma increased significantly (from 6.4 ± 0.7 mV to 25.9 ± 3.1 mV) as the uncaging site moved from distal (318.6 ± 7.9 µm) to proximal (99 ± 14.6 µm) dendritic locations (Figure 4c; p = 0.00014).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The apical dendrites of PCx pyramidal neurons are capable of generating spikes throughout the layers that receive LOT and IC inputs.
claims.source: Thus, the apical dendrites of PCx pyramidal neurons are capable of generating spikes throughout the layers that receive LOT and IC inputs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data.

claims.claim: When dendritic spikes were initiated at distal dendritic locations using synaptic stimulation (254.85 ± 14.95 µm from soma), addition of baclofen only slightly altered spike amplitude (spike amplitude was reduced by 10.4 ± 7.3%, p = 0.02 and spike threshold increased by 10.1 ± 12.6%, p = 0.004, n = 6).
claims.source: When dendritic spikes were initiated at distal dendritic locations using synaptic stimulation (254.85 ± 14.95 µm from soma), addition of baclofen only slightly altered spike amplitude (Figure 4d–e; spike amplitude was reduced by 10.4 ± 7.3%, p = 0.02 and spike threshold increased by 10.1 ± 12.6%, p = 0.004, n = 6).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: At mid dendritic locations (197.3 ± 12 µm), local spikes were evidently triggered by a mixture of LOT and intracortical inputs, since upon baclofen application, response amplitude was reduced (peak voltage response was reduced by 42.0 ± 13.3%, compared to control; n = 6).
claims.source: At mid dendritic locations (197.3 ± 12 µm), local spikes were evidently triggered by a mixture of LOT and intracortical inputs, since upon baclofen application, response amplitude was reduced (peak voltage response was reduced by 42.0 ± 13.3%, compared to control; n = 6).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation with quantitative measurements and interpretation.

claims.claim: At more proximal locations (161.6 ± 9.6 µm) spike initiation was almost completely dependent on intracortical inputs: when baclofen was present, we were unable to initiate local spikes at all, and the voltage response was significantly reduced (peak response was reduced by 63.2 ± 6.2%, compared to control; n = 6).
claims.source: At more proximal locations (161.6 ± 9.6 µm) spike initiation was almost completely dependent on intracortical inputs: when baclofen was present, we were unable to initiate local spikes at all, and the voltage response was significantly reduced (Figure 4f–g; peak response was reduced by 63.2 ± 6.2%, compared to control; n = 6).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation with quantitative measurements and interpretation.

claims.claim: At all dendritic locations, addition of APV (50 µm) completely abolished spike initiation.
claims.source: At all dendritic locations, addition of APV (50 µm) completely abolished spike initiation (Figure 4d–h).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Pyramidal neurons in PCx are capable of NMDA spike generation throughout their apical arbors.
claims.source: Taken together these results indicate that pyramidal neurons in PCx are capable of NMDA spike generation throughout their apical arbors; that both LOT and IC inputs can generate NMDA spikes within their respective layers; and that these synaptically evoked dendritic spikes show the commonly observed increase in amplitude as the initiation site moves closer to the soma (Major et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data.

claims.claim: Both LOT and IC inputs can generate NMDA spikes within their respective layers.
claims.source: Taken together these results indicate that pyramidal neurons in PCx are capable of NMDA spike generation throughout their apical arbors; that both LOT and IC inputs can generate NMDA spikes within their respective layers; and that these synaptically evoked dendritic spikes show the commonly observed increase in amplitude as the initiation site moves closer to the soma (Major et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data.

claims.claim: Synaptically evoked dendritic spikes show the commonly observed increase in amplitude as the initiation site moves closer to the soma.
claims.source: Taken together these results indicate that pyramidal neurons in PCx are capable of NMDA spike generation throughout their apical arbors; that both LOT and IC inputs can generate NMDA spikes within their respective layers; and that these synaptically evoked dendritic spikes show the commonly observed increase in amplitude as the initiation site moves closer to the soma (Major et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data and supported by citation.

claims.claim: Coactivation of two inputs on the same dendrite resulted in a strong nonlinear interaction, where Input two significantly lowered the threshold for local spike generation by Input 1 (by 46.55 ± 1.8% for peak voltage; t-test p < 0.0001 and 52 degrees of freedom; F-score of 2.36).
claims.source: Coactivation of the two inputs resulted in a strong nonlinear interaction, where Input two significantly lowered the threshold for local spike generation by Input 1 (by 46.55 ± 1.8% for peak voltage; t-test p < 0.0001 and 52 degrees of freedom; F-score of 2.36; Figure 5a–d) without changing the response peak amplitude.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The nonlinear interaction between LOT inputs delivered to two different branches, even when those branches were 'sisters', was much weaker than the within-branch interaction, as evidenced by the much smaller change in spike threshold caused by the bias input (7.98 ± 0.75%, n = 5 threshold change for the sister-branch and 6.28 ± 1.88%, n = 6 threshold change for the different-branch).
claims.source: We found in favor of this hypothesis, that the nonlinear interaction between LOT inputs delivered to two different branches, even when those branches were 'sisters' (Figure 5c–e), was much weaker than the within-branch interaction, as evidenced by the much smaller change in spike threshold caused by the bias input (7.98 ± 0.75%, n = 5 threshold change for the sister-branch and 6.28 ± 1.88%, n = 6 threshold change for the different-branch, Figure 5c–e).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claims.claim: An ANOVA test for comparison between the three groups (same, sister, different branches) showed statistical significance (p < 0.01).
claims.source: An ANOVA test for comparison between the three groups (same, sister, different branches) showed statistical significance (p < 0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: Post-hoc analysis (Tukey-Kramer test) comparing each group with every other group yielded significant differences between same branch and sister and different branches (p < 0.01), but no statistical significance between sister and different branches (p = 0.98).
claims.source: Post-hoc analysis (Tukey-Kramer test) comparing each group with every other group yielded significant differences between same branch and sister and different branches (p < 0.01), but no statistical significance between sister and different branches (p = 0.98).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical analysis of experimental data.

claims.claim: In the pairing experiments in the presence of APV, the bias added a roughly constant value to the unpaired voltage response (Control + APV) all along the curve, confirming that without NMDA channels, pyramidal neuron dendrites revert to roughly linear summation.
claims.source: To more closely examine the role of NMDA channels in the pairing outcomes, we repeated the pairing experiments in the presence of APV (Figure 5c–d). In these cases, the bias added a roughly constant value to the unpaired voltage response (Control + APV) all along the curve, confirming that without NMDA channels, pyramidal neuron dendrites revert to roughly linear summation.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation and interpretation.

claims.claim: The threshold was lowered by 52.2 ± 2.34% and 15.6 ± 4.2% when the synaptic bias was located on the same or different branches, respectively, in glutamate uncaging experiments.
claims.source: Similar to the previous two-electrode summation experiments, we observed a significant difference between same and different branch summation. The threshold was lowered by 52.2 ± 2.34% and 15.6 ± 4.2% when the synaptic bias was located on the same or different branches, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claims.claim: NMDA spike generation in the distal apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons provides the superlinearity needed to enforce selectivity for specific combinations of LOT inputs.
claims.source: Together these results support a model of olfactory coding in PCx in which (1) NMDA spike generation in the distal apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons provides the superlinearity needed to enforce selectivity for specific combinations of LOT inputs, while the compartmentalization of voltage signals in the apical tree allows for different LOT combinations to be mapped onto different apical dendrites with relatively little crosstalk between them.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data and modeling.

claims.claim: The compartmentalization of voltage signals in the apical tree allows for different LOT combinations to be mapped onto different apical dendrites with relatively little crosstalk between them.
claims.source: Together these results support a model of olfactory coding in PCx in which (1) NMDA spike generation in the distal apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons provides the superlinearity needed to enforce selectivity for specific combinations of LOT inputs, while the compartmentalization of voltage signals in the apical tree allows for different LOT combinations to be mapped onto different apical dendrites with relatively little crosstalk between them.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental data and modeling.

claims.claim: Summation of LOT and IC inputs was very similar in form to the summation of two inputs confined to the LOT: the IC bias input again led to a substantial threshold reduction for LOT inputs (35.44 ± 2.0%, n = 15), with no increase in response magnitude.
claims.source: We found that summation of LOT and IC inputs was very similar in form to the summation of two inputs confined to the LOT (Figure 6a–e): the IC bias input again led to a substantial threshold reduction for LOT inputs (35.44 ± 2.0%, n = 15), with no increase in response magnitude.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claims.claim: The threshold-lowering effect of the bias input was relatively constant within increasing separation of the two inputs, indicating that over much of its length, a pyramidal neuron apical dendrite functions as a single, relatively location-insensitive integrative subunit.
claims.source: Indeed, the threshold-lowering effect of the bias input was relatively constant within increasing separation of the two inputs (Figure 6f), indicating that over much of its length, a pyramidal neuron apical dendrite functions as a single, relatively location-insensitive integrative subunit.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data.

claims.claim: Blocking NMDARs linearized the input-output curves, destroying their sigmoidal form, and eliminating the basis for a superlinear within–branch interactions.
claims.source: We also found that, just as for pairs of inputs confined to the LOT, the nonlinear interaction between LOT and IC inputs depended completely on NMDA regenerativity: blocking NMDARs linearized the input-output curves, destroying their sigmoidal form, and eliminating the basis for a superlinear within–branch interactions (Figure 6, grey curves).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation and interpretation.

claims.claim: When the bias was provided by an IC input on a sister branch, the nonlinear interaction was evident, though significantly weaker compared to that seen with a same-branch IC bias (threshold reduction was 23.38 ± 2.34%, n = 8).
claims.source: When the bias was provided by an IC input on a sister branch, the nonlinear interaction was evident, though significantly weaker compared to that seen with a same-branch IC bias (Figure 7a–b,e). Threshold reduction was 23.38 ± 2.34% (n = 8) for IC locations on sister branches and 18.4 ± 2.88% (n = 7) for IC bias on different branch (Figure 7c–e).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claims.claim: Threshold reduction was 18.4 ± 2.88% (n = 7) for IC bias on different branch.
claims.source: Threshold reduction was 23.38 ± 2.34% (n = 8) for IC locations on sister branches and 18.4 ± 2.88% (n = 7) for IC bias on different branch (Figure 7c–e).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from experimental data.

claims.claim: The model cell can generate NMDA spikes in response to concentrated synaptic excitation at any location along a pyramidal neuron's apical dendrite.
claims.source: We first established that the model cell can generate NMDA spikes in response to concentrated synaptic excitation at any location along a pyramidal neuron's apical dendrite, and that both the threshold for spike initiation and the spike amplitude measured at the soma increase as the site of spike initiation moves closer to the soma (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: Both the threshold for spike initiation and the spike amplitude measured at the soma increase as the site of spike initiation moves closer to the soma in the model.
claims.source: We first established that the model cell can generate NMDA spikes in response to concentrated synaptic excitation at any location along a pyramidal neuron's apical dendrite, and that both the threshold for spike initiation and the spike amplitude measured at the soma increase as the site of spike initiation moves closer to the soma (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: The model supports the experimental finding that nonlinear synaptic summation of LOT inputs to distal apical dendrites is strongly compartmentalized, with individual apical dendrites acting as well-separated integrative subunits.
claims.source: Thus, the model supports our experimental finding that nonlinear synaptic summation of LOT inputs to distal apical dendrites is strongly compartmentalized, with individual apical dendrites acting as well-separated integrative subunits.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from computational modeling results.

claims.claim: The model replicated the experimental finding that IC bias inputs on sister and different branches had a significantly weaker effect than an IC bias on the same branch.
claims.source: In addition, the model replicated the experimental finding that IC bias inputs on sister and different branches had a significantly weaker effect than an IC bias on the same branch (compare Figure 8—figure supplement 2g to Figure 8d), though the degree of compartmentalization of IC inputs was, as in the experiments, and as expected from passive cable theory, less pronounced than the compartmentalization of LOT inputs.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling that replicates experimental results.

claims.claim: The degree of compartmentalization of IC inputs was less pronounced than the compartmentalization of LOT inputs.
claims.source: In addition, the model replicated the experimental finding that IC bias inputs on sister and different branches had a significantly weaker effect than an IC bias on the same branch (compare Figure 8—figure supplement 2g to Figure 8d), though the degree of compartmentalization of IC inputs was, as in the experiments, and as expected from passive cable theory, less pronounced than the compartmentalization of LOT inputs.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling and experimental data.

claims.claim: Simulations revealed strong supralinear LOT and IC input summation when either of the inputs was temporally shifted by 20 ms, and in some cases more.
claims.source: These nonlinear synaptic interactions persisted for non-synchronized inputs: our simulations revealed strong supralinear LOT and IC input summation when either of the inputs was temporally shifted by 20 ms, and in some cases more (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: The model supports the experimental findings that IC inputs interact nonlinearly with LOT inputs over extended spatio-temporal scales.
claims.source: Thus, the model supports our experimental findings that IC inputs interact nonlinearly with LOT inputs over extended spatio-temporal scales.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from computational modeling results.

claims.claim: Clustered LOT inputs reliably evoked NMDA spikes, powerfully amplifying postsynaptic signal compared to Ohmic (voltage-independent) NMDAR.
claims.source: As predicted, we found that that clustered LOT inputs reliably evoked NMDA spikes, powerfully amplifying postsynaptic signal compared to Ohmic (voltage-independent) NMDAR (Figure 8c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: Dispersed LOT activation typically failed to overcome the local spike threshold on any dendrite, due both to the lack of concentrated excitation and the presence of inhibition, and therefore resulted in significantly smaller local dendritic and somatic voltage responses.
claims.source: In contrast, dispersed LOT activation typically failed to overcome the local spike threshold on any dendrite, due both to the lack of concentrated excitation and the presence of inhibition, and therefore resulted in significantly smaller local dendritic and somatic voltage responses (Figure 8b–d, pink).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: The difference between clustered and dispersed synaptic distributions was evident over a large input range, leading to preferential amplification of input combinations that target individual postsynaptic branches.
claims.source: The difference between clustered and dispersed synaptic distributions was evident over a large input range (Figure 8c–d), leading to preferential amplification of input combinations that target individual postsynaptic branches (Figure 8c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: Stimulation with Ohmic NMDARs eliminated the strong dependence of postsynaptic responses on the spatial distribution of synaptic inputs.
claims.source: This effect was entirely dependent on regenerative NMDAR currents: stimulation with Ohmic NMDARs, eliminated the strong dependence of postsynaptic responses on the spatial distribution of synaptic inputs (Figure 8c, inset,).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: The AB combination produced strong supralinear responses, whereas the AC combination produced only a weak depolarization and mostly linear or sublinear summation in the model.
claims.source: We found the AB combination produced strong supralinear responses (Figure 8f left, g, black), whereas the AC combination produced only a weak depolarization and mostly linear or sublinear summation (Figure 8f, right, g, pink).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claims.claim: Even in the presence of significant trial-to-trial variability introduced by random background activity and biologically-realistic presynaptic firing patterns, the model olfactory pyramidal neuron was able to use clustered glomerular activation as a basis for representing certain 'odor' combinations but not others.
claims.source: Thus, even in the presence of significant trial-to-trial variability introduced by random background activity and biologically-realistic presynaptic firing patterns, the model olfactory pyramidal neuron was able to use clustered glomerular activation as a basis for representing certain 'odor' combinations but not others (Figure 8h).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from computational modeling results.

claims.claim: Pyramidal neurons in PCx can generate local spikes throughout their apical dendrites.

results.result: NMDA spikes can be generated in dendrites of PCx pyramidal neurons through glutamate uncaging. These spikes are mediated primarily by NMDAR channels, with minimal contribution from voltage-gated sodium and calcium channels, as demonstrated by pharmacological blockade experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C31 provide converging pharmacological evidence showing that dendritic spikes evoked by glutamate uncaging are abolished by APV (NMDAR blocker) but not significantly affected by TTX or calcium channel blockers. The experimental design with progressive laser intensity and systematic pharmacological dissection provides strong support for NMDA-mediated dendritic spikes.

results.result: Synaptic activation of LOT inputs can trigger NMDA spikes in PCx pyramidal neurons with characteristic threshold (14.1±1.6 mV), amplitude (27.1±2.4 mV), and area (3817.8±396.9 mV*ms) measured at the soma. APV blocks these spikes and linearizes stimulus-response curves.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 provide quantitative measurements with appropriate sample sizes (n=48 cells for baseline, n=17 for APV) and statistical analysis. The pharmacological validation with APV confirms NMDA dependence. The measurements are internally consistent and well-documented.

results.result: Intracellular application of MK801 blocks NMDA spikes, reducing spike amplitude and area to 32.7±5.3% and 17.2±2.2% respectively, demonstrating that NMDA regenerativity is postsynaptic rather than network-mediated.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 provide critical evidence distinguishing postsynaptic NMDA regenerativity from network effects. The intracellular MK801 approach is methodologically sound and the quantitative reductions are substantial and well-measured (n=6 cells, 40 min after breakthrough).

results.result: NMDA spikes are accompanied by large, localized calcium transients that peak at the activated dendritic site and fall off steeply in both directions, indicating local, non-actively propagated spikes similar to those in other pyramidal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 provide calcium imaging evidence consistent with localized NMDA spike generation. The spatial profile of calcium transients (steep falloff, confinement to stimulated branches) supports the interpretation of compartmentalized dendritic spikes, with appropriate comparison to literature (C46).

results.result: NMDA spikes can be generated throughout the apical dendrites of PCx pyramidal neurons in all layers (1a, 1b, and 2). Both LOT and IC inputs can generate NMDA spikes in their respective layers, with spike amplitude increasing as initiation sites move closer to the soma.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C57 demonstrate NMDA spike generation across dendritic locations with systematic baclofen experiments (C51-C53) showing layer-specific input contributions. The distance-dependent amplitude increase (C49: p=0.00014) and complete APV blockade (C54) provide strong support. Sample sizes are adequate (n=6 per condition).

results.result: Coactivation of two LOT inputs on the same dendrite produces strong nonlinear interactions (46.55±1.8% threshold reduction), while inputs on different branches show much weaker interactions (7.98±0.75% for sister branches, 6.28±1.88% for different branches). This compartmentalization depends on NMDA channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 provide quantitative evidence for dendritic compartmentalization with appropriate statistical analysis (ANOVA p<0.01, post-hoc tests). The ~10-fold difference between same-branch and between-branch interactions is substantial. APV experiments (C62) confirm NMDA dependence. The experimental design systematically tests the compartmentalization hypothesis.

results.result: NMDA spike generation in distal apical dendrites provides the superlinearity needed to enforce selectivity for specific combinations of LOT inputs, while dendritic compartmentalization allows different dendrites to represent different odorant combinations with minimal crosstalk.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 represent a synthesis of the experimental findings (C58-C63) into a mechanistic model. The conclusion is well-supported by the compartmentalization data and nonlinear summation experiments, though it represents an interpretive framework rather than direct measurement.

results.result: LOT and IC inputs summate nonlinearly on the same dendrite, with IC bias inputs producing substantial threshold reduction (35.44±2.0%) that is relatively constant over distance. This nonlinearity depends completely on NMDA regenerativity.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 demonstrate nonlinear LOT-IC interactions with adequate sample size (n=15). The distance-independence of threshold reduction (C67) is an important finding supported by Figure 6f. APV linearization (C68) confirms NMDA dependence.

results.result: IC inputs on sister or different branches produce weaker nonlinear interactions (23.38±2.34% and 18.4±2.88% threshold reduction respectively) compared to same-branch IC inputs, indicating softer compartmentalization of IC inputs compared to LOT inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 provide quantitative measurements showing IC inputs are less compartmentalized than LOT inputs. Sample sizes are adequate (n=8 for sister, n=7 for different branches). The finding is consistent with passive cable theory expectations discussed in the manuscript.

results.result: Computational modeling replicates experimental findings, showing that the model cell generates NMDA spikes throughout apical dendrites with distance-dependent properties, strong compartmentalization of LOT inputs, softer compartmentalization of IC inputs, and persistent nonlinear interactions over temporal delays up to 20ms.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 describe modeling results that closely replicate experimental findings. The model validation strengthens the experimental conclusions by demonstrating consistency with biophysical principles. The temporal integration findings (C76) extend beyond the experimental data but are plausible given NMDA kinetics.

results.result: In the computational model with in vivo-like conditions, clustered LOT inputs reliably evoke NMDA spikes and produce larger responses than dispersed inputs. The model demonstrates that neurons can respond selectively to certain glomerular combinations (AB) but not others (AC) based on dendritic clustering.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C83 demonstrate the functional consequences of NMDA spikes and compartmentalization in a realistic model with background activity and physiological firing patterns. The AB vs AC discrimination (C82-C83, n=1000 trials, p<10^-9) provides strong computational evidence for discontinuous receptive fields. The model includes appropriate biological constraints.

results.result: The 2-layer integrative behavior of olfactory pyramidal neuron dendrites, involving NMDA spike amplification and compartmentalization, provides a mechanism for the nonlinear remapping of the odor code from olfactory bulb to piriform cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing the experimental and modeling results into a coherent framework. These claims are well-supported by the collective evidence from pharmacology, electrophysiology, calcium imaging, and modeling (C21-C83).

results.result: PCx pyramidal neurons implement a 2-layer computation where individual dendrites sum inputs linearly up to threshold (layer 1), then outputs from separately thresholded dendrites combine linearly at the soma (layer 2). This architecture enables selective responses to specific high-order odorant combinations, potentially explaining discontinuous receptive fields.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93 articulate the computational framework emerging from the experimental data. The 2-layer model is well-supported by the compartmentalization experiments and nonlinear summation data. The connection to discontinuous receptive fields (C93) is appropriately qualified as a potential explanation with supporting citations.

results.result: The current findings showing NMDA regenerativity and 2-layer summation logic in PCx pyramidal neurons are inconsistent with Bathellier et al. 2009, which reported linear integration in these neurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 accurately identifies a discrepancy with prior work. The authors acknowledge this inconsistency and provide methodological speculation about potential causes (distributed vs. focal stimulation). The current study's extensive pharmacological and biophysical characterization provides strong evidence for NMDA spikes, though the reason for the discrepancy remains uncertain.

results.result: The properties of NMDA spikes and the logic of synaptic integration in PCx pyramidal neurons, including NMDAR-mediated spikes and pronounced same-branch vs. between-branch summation differences, are consistent with findings in pyramidal neurons from other cortical areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C87 place the findings in the context of the broader literature on dendritic integration. The comparisons are well-supported by appropriate citations and the experimental data demonstrating similar biophysical properties across cortical regions.

results.result: Dendritic thresholding nonlinearity provided by regenerative NMDA currents can mediate the supralinear integration of LOT inputs observed in previous in vitro and in vivo studies.
results.evaluation: Claim C103 connects the current findings to prior observations of supralinear LOT integration. The claim is well-supported by the experimental demonstration of NMDA-dependent nonlinearity and is appropriately framed as supporting an idea rather than proving it definitively.

results.result: Quantitatively, the threshold-lowering power of a second LOT input on the same branch is roughly 10 times that of an LOT input on a different branch, while for IC inputs this ratio is only 2-fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 provide quantitative summaries of the compartmentalization differences between LOT and IC inputs. These are well-supported by the experimental data in Figures 5-7 and represent important quantitative characterizations of dendritic integration.

results.result: The nonlinear interaction of LOT and IC inputs mediated by NMDA regenerativity could provide a biophysical mechanism for binding odor with contextual information in piriform cortex.
results.evaluation: Claim C110 is speculative and extends beyond the experimental data. While the nonlinear LOT-IC interactions are well-demonstrated (C66-C70), the functional role in binding odor with context is a hypothesis that would require additional experiments to test. The claim is appropriately qualified with 'could provide.'

results.result: NMDA spikes could serve as local induction signals for plasticity of LOT synapses, with groups of co-active LOT synapses on the same dendrite potentially triggering local LTP.
results.evaluation: Claims C113 and C115 are speculative hypotheses about plasticity mechanisms. While the localized calcium transients (C112) provide plausibility, no plasticity experiments were performed. The claims are appropriately qualified as speculative and supported by analogy to CA3 neurons (C114), but require experimental validation.

results.result: Background on olfactory system organization: PCx receives direct input from olfactory bulb and is the main station for odor recognition. Mitral/tufted cells respond to individual odorant molecules while PCx pyramidal neurons respond to multiple, apparently random combinations of activated glomeruli. The connectivity between OB and PCx lacks spatial structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C16 provide established background knowledge about the olfactory system, supported by appropriate citations. These claims accurately represent the current understanding of olfactory processing and connectivity patterns.

results.result: Spontaneous spike-like events resembling synaptically evoked NMDA spikes were occasionally observed, with amplitude 17.78±2.09 mV and area 9941±2640 mV*ms (n=22 spikes).
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C40 document spontaneous events resembling NMDA spikes. The observation is well-characterized quantitatively, though the sample size (n=22 spikes) and occasional nature suggest this is a supplementary finding rather than a central result.

results.result: IC inputs are closer to branch points where sister and cousin dendrites connect, so their effects are felt more widely, as predicted by passive cable theory.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 provides a mechanistic explanation for the softer compartmentalization of IC inputs based on cable theory. This is a reasonable interpretation supported by the anatomical organization and the experimental observations of IC input integration.

results.result: The degree of nonlinear crosstalk between dendritic branches may be overestimated in subthreshold summation experiments compared to cells operating in the firing regime, because somatic spike generation acts as a time-averaged voltage clamp suppressing subthreshold voltage communication between dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C108 cite prior work (Behabadi and Mel, 2014) to provide an important caveat about interpreting the IC compartmentalization results. This is a valid methodological consideration that appropriately qualifies the conclusions about IC input integration.

results.result: Compartmentalized NMDA spikes in pyramidal neuron dendrites could provide both thresholding nonlinearity for combination selectivity and amplification for distal inputs to drive somatic action potentials.
results.evaluation: Claim C17 presents the initial hypothesis that motivated the study. This hypothesis is well-grounded in prior literature (multiple citations) and is subsequently validated by the experimental results. The claim appropriately frames the hypothesis as a 'possible mechanism.'

results.result: Prior studies by Bathellier et al. 2009 and Apicella et al. 2010 reported findings that appeared inconsistent with NMDA-mediated dendritic integration: Bathellier et al. found insufficient regenerative currents and linear summation, while Apicella et al. found that combination selectivity did not depend on IC inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C20 accurately represent findings from prior studies that created a 'conundrum' motivating the current work. The citations are appropriate and the characterization of prior results appears accurate based on the referenced papers.

results.result: Background on odor coding transformation: The anatomical projection from OB to PCx is assumed to be random. Different odors activate unique, distributed sets of PCx neurons. The transformation from molecule-specific responses in glomeruli to multi-combination selectivity in PCx requires nonlinearity. Prior studies showed supralinear LOT integration that doesn't require bulb interactions or IC inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C102 provide important background on odor coding and prior findings about nonlinear integration. These claims are well-supported by appropriate citations and accurately represent the state of knowledge that motivated the current study.

results.result: IC inputs provide contextual information from higher-order cortical regions including entorhinal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex, and amygdala, potentially allowing assignment of cognitive and emotional value to odors.
results.evaluation: Claim C109 describes the functional role of IC inputs based on anatomical connectivity. This is well-supported by citations and provides important context for understanding the significance of LOT-IC interactions demonstrated in the study.

results.result: Backpropagating action potentials in PCx pyramidal neuron apical dendrites attenuate significantly, making them less likely to contribute to STDP of distal LOT synapses. In contrast, NMDA currents produce large localized calcium transients (±20 µm) that could serve as local plasticity signals.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 combine cited prior work on bAP attenuation with the current study's calcium imaging data to make an argument about plasticity mechanisms. The logic is sound and the calcium imaging data (C43-C45) support the spatial localization claim.

results.result: NMDA spikes contribute to long-term potentiation in dendrites of CA3 neurons, as shown by Brandalise and Gerber, 2014.
results.evaluation: Claim C114 accurately cites prior work demonstrating a role for NMDA spikes in plasticity in a different brain region. This citation provides support by analogy for the speculation about plasticity in PCx (C113, C115).
